newsitem.title: USA: US GDP 3.4 pct next 4 qtrs-Cleveland Fed economist.
newsitem.headline: US GDP 3.4 pct next 4 qtrs-Cleveland Fed economist.

text.p: The steep U.S. Treasury yield curve predicts the U.S. Gross Domestic Product would grow by an average 3.4 percent over the next four quarters, according to a study by a senior economist of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland.

"Given a current spread of around 160 basis points, the yield curve would predict U.S. real GDP growth averaging about 3.4 percent over the next four quarters," Cleveland Fed economist Joseph Haubrich -- who co-authored the study with Cleveland Fed analyst Ann Dombrosky -- told Reuters.

Haubrich's and Dombrosky's work draws from previous yield curve studies, including a paper by New York Fed Director of Research Frederic Mishkin and senior vice president Arturo Estrella, published in June.
The Mishkin-Estrella model uses the same yield spread sample as Haubrich's and covers a similar period, 1960-1995.
Mishkin and Estrella concluded the yield curve is an excellent predictor of changes in the business cycle.
In June, their model showed an almost zero probability of a U.S. recession over the next four quarters. With the yield curve spread little changed since, that forecast holds.

The Haubrich-Dombrosky paper is based on the relationship between the Treasury yield curve behavior and the U.S. economy's performance in 1961-1995. The spread used is the three-month T-bill yield equivalent/10-year T-note yield.

"The yield curve is definitely steeper than its historical average, which means better-than-average economic growth ahead," said Haubrich, noting the average three-month/10-year Treasury spread "is about 120 basis points."
The three-month T-bill opened on Monday at a yield equivalent of 5.03 percent while the 10-year note yielded 6.68 percent for a 165 basis-point spread.
Haubrich said he took the Mishkin-Estrella work one step further -- to test the curve's ability to forecast actual GDP levels as opposed to boom-bust cycles only.

Among the theories supporting this specific forecasting ability of the yield curve, Haubrich cited the "expectations hypothesis... (when) long-term interest rates are the average of expected future short-term rates," as well as the "policy anticipation hypothesis... (when) the yield curve picks up the financial market's estimate of future policy."
Haubrich also suggested the yield curve may respond to monetary policy changes at the same time the economy does.

"Current monetary policy may shift both the yield curve and future output," Haubrich said. "Monetary policy may react to output so that the yield curve picks up a complex intermingling of policy actions, reactions and real effects."

The Cleveland Fed model shows the yield curve as a good GDP forecaster tool for 35 years during which the U.S. economy experienced five recessions, and inflation fluctuated between 1.0 percent and 13.0 percent-plus and the federal funds rate between less than 3.0 percent and more than 19.0 percent.
However, Haubrich acknowledged the yield curve has proved to be a less reliable forecaster in the past 10 years.

"The yield curve is a good predictor of future GDP growth but we have to be cautious because the relationship between the economy and the yield curve has changed over time," he said. "We are in a different type of economy, with a different type of industries."
Haubrich cautioned against relying on data going too far back to forecast future growth because of the major technology changes the U.S. economy experienced in the past decade.
Though both New York and Cleveland Fed's yield curve models predict healthy growth ahead, their work does not represent the Fed's official view.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan told Congress in July the Federal Open Market Committee's GDP forecast was 2-1/2 to 2-3/4 percent in 1996 and 1-3/4 to 2-1/4 percent in 1997.
